subject: body
title: Taste and Trying New Foods
about: How tasting works (the tongue and its taste buds, sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory, and the nose doing half the job), textures, trying a new food ten or more times with one polite bite, foods from different families and countries, being kind about what others eat, and dips and growing a vegetable to make trying fun. NC 1.NPA.1.2 (exploring a variety of foods) with 1.NPA.1.3 (where foods come from) and 1.ICHR.1.2 (respecting the ways families and friends are different, including what they eat); the senses part is a bridge topic. Read it together, and bring a lemon slice and a pretzel to taste as you go.
tip: Serve one new food next to two favorites and ask only for one polite bite; no pressure after that.

cards.q: Stick out your tongue and look in a mirror. What are the tiny bumps all over it for?
cards.note: The bumps have a big name, papillae. Hiding inside them are your taste buds.

cards.q: Sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and one more. The fifth taste, in soup broth and cheese, is called...?
cards.note: Savory is also called umami, and you taste it in broth, tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese. Spicy is not a taste at all; it is your tongue feeling heat.

cards.q: Sweet, salty, sour and bitter are four kinds of...?
cards.note: Your taste buds sort every bite into these tastes and send the news to your brain. Most foods are a mix of more than one.

cards.q: You lick a lemon and your face scrunches up. Which taste is that?
cards.note: Lemons, limes and pickles are sour. Sour makes your mouth water.

cards.q: You eat a pretzel. Which taste do you get?
cards.note: Pretzels, chips, olives and soy sauce are salty. Salt also hides in soup and cheese.

cards.q: You bite a cookie. Which taste is that?
cards.note: Sugar, honey and ripe fruit taste sweet. Babies like sweet best, and that is normal.

cards.q: Kale and other leafy greens have a strong taste many grown-ups like. Which taste is it?
cards.note: Bitter is the taste kids often need the most tries to like. Many grown-ups love it.

cards.q: Pinch your nose shut and eat a bite of apple. What happens to the taste?
cards.note: Most of what we call flavor is really smell, which is why food tastes dull when you have a cold. Let go of your nose and the apple flavor rushes back.

cards.q: You try a new food and are unsure about it. How many tries can it take to like a new food?
cards.note: Taste buds learn: the first bite is a stranger, and by the tenth it is a friend. Keep offering, no pressure.

cards.q: A new food is on your plate. What does a polite bite look like?
cards.note: One polite bite means trying a small taste. After that you can say no thank you to more.

cards.q: Your friend's lunch looks and smells different from yours. What is the kind thing to say?
cards.note: Everyone's taste buds are different, so do not yuck someone's yum. Curious and kind is the way.

cards.q: Tacos, sushi and pasta come from different...?
cards.note: Tacos come from Mexico, sushi from Japan, pasta from Italy. Trying them is like a tasty trip.

cards.q: Your family's dinner and your friend's dinner are different. What does that show?
cards.note: Every family has its own foods and traditions. Different is interesting, never wrong.

cards.q: Carrots and crackers go crunch. What do we call the way a food feels in your mouth?
cards.note: Crunchy, soft, smooth, chewy and crispy are textures. Some kids like crunchy best.

cards.q: Mashed potatoes and yogurt feel smooth and soft. Is that a taste or a texture?
cards.note: Taste is sweet or salty; texture is how food feels. You can like a food's taste but need time to get used to its texture.

cards.q: You grow a tomato plant and pick the tomatoes yourself. How does that change eating them?
cards.note: Kids who grow or cook a food are much more likely to taste it. Try a pot of cherry tomatoes or herbs.

cards.q: A new food is hard to try plain. What can make it easier?
cards.note: Dip broccoli in ranch or hummus, or pair a new food with an old favorite. Small tricks help.
